title: Hard brake pedal
h1: Why is my brake pedal hard to press?
metaDesc: Brake pedal hard to push or car hard to stop? See if it's the brake booster, a vacuum leak, an engine stall or worn brakes, and how urgent it is.
synonyms: brake pedal stiff and car won't stop
have to stand on the brakes
brake pedal hard when engine off
intro: Your brakes use engine vacuum, a pump or an electric unit to multiply the force of your foot. When that help (the brake booster) stops working, the pedal turns hard and the car takes much more effort to stop. A hard pedal can also be normal with the engine off. A few questions will tell you which, and how urgent it is.
safety: If you have to press with all your strength to slow down, pull over when it's safe and stop driving.
If the engine stalls while you're driving, braking may take much more force. Press firmly and steadily rather than pumping, and get it checked before driving further.
If the steering also becomes very heavy, pull over and stop.

q_severity.help: The brake booster is the round canister behind the brake pedal, on the driver's side of the engine bay. It makes the pedal easier to press.

opts.a: Only when the engine is off, before I start it
It went hard after the engine stalled or shut off while driving
All the time with the engine running, and I can barely stop the car
It's stiffer than usual, but the car stops if I push harder
The pedal feels normal, but the car takes longer to stop

q_clues.q: Do you notice either of these as well?

opts.a: A hissing sound when I press the pedal, or the idle stumbles when I brake
The steering has also become heavy (common on trucks and diesels)
Neither of these / I'm not sure
The brakes were just replaced (new pads or rotors)
The brakes got very hot, like on a long downhill or while towing, and I smell burning
The car also pulls to one side when braking
There's oil or fluid on the inside of a wheel
None of these / I'm not sure

result.title: A hard pedal with the engine off is usually normal
result.now: Start the engine with your foot on the brake. The pedal should drop slightly and then feel normal.
if: If the pedal doesn't drop when the engine starts, the brake booster or its vacuum supply may have a problem. Have the brakes checked within a few days.
If the pedal is still hard once the engine is running, treat it as a brake fault and don't drive until it's checked.
If the pedal sinks toward the floor with the engine running, or the red brake light is on, don't drive it.
result.why: The brake booster stores enough vacuum for one or two assisted presses after the engine stops. Once that's used up, the pedal feels hard until the engine runs again. That's how most systems are designed to work.

causes.name: Normal booster behavior with the engine off
causes.clues: The pedal is hard only before starting, and feels normal once the engine runs.

causes.name: Weak booster or leaking check valve
causes.clues: The pedal doesn't drop at start-up, or the assist runs out right after you shut the engine off.

you: With the engine off, press the pedal several times until it's hard. Hold it down and start the engine. The pedal should sink slightly.
shop: Brake booster and check valve test

result.title: The engine shutting off may have taken away your brake assist
result.now: Once you're safely stopped, set the parking brake and don't drive it. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic find out why the engine stalled.
if: If it restarts and the pedal feels normal again, an engine that stalls while driving still isn't safe. Have it checked before driving any distance.
If the pedal stays hard with the engine running, or sinks, or the red brake light is on, don't drive it.
If the temperature gauge was high or you saw steam before it stalled, don't restart it.
result.why: Most brake boosters rely on the running engine. When the engine dies, you may get one or two assisted presses, then the pedal turns hard and braking takes much more force. Steering assist may be lost too. The stall is the problem to find, and the brakes should be checked along with it.

causes.name: Fuel or ignition problem
causes.clues: Sputtering before it died, or a check engine light.

causes.name: Idle control problem
causes.clues: It stalls when slowing down or coming to a stop.

causes.name: Charging system failure
causes.clues: The battery light came on before the engine died.

you: Note any warning lights that came on before it stalled.
Note whether it stalled while slowing down or at speed.

result.title: Your brakes may have lost their power assist
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and stop driving. Have it towed or have a mobile mechanic come to you.
if: If you hear a loud hiss when you press the pedal, tell the shop. It points to a torn booster or a disconnected vacuum hose.
If a brake system warning message is on (common on hybrids and electric cars), have it towed to a shop equipped for your model.
If the pedal sinks toward the floor or the red brake light is on, don't move the car at all.
result.why: With working assist, light pressure stops the car. Without it, you need far more force and the stopping distance grows, which is dangerous in an emergency stop. Common causes are a failed booster, a cracked or disconnected vacuum hose, or loss of whatever powers the booster.

causes.name: Cracked or disconnected vacuum hose
causes.clues: It happened suddenly, with hissing or a rough idle.

causes.name: Failed brake booster
causes.clues: Hissing from under the dash near the pedal, and the pedal doesn't drop when the engine starts.

causes.name: Failed vacuum pump or electric brake booster
causes.clues: A diesel, some turbocharged engines, a hybrid or an electric car, often with a warning message.

causes.name: Hydraulic booster or power steering problem
causes.clues: A truck or diesel, and the steering got heavy too.

you: With the car parked and in Park, listen for a hiss near the pedal or under the hood as you press the brake.
shop: Vacuum supply and check valve test
Code scan on cars with electric boosters

result.title: A vacuum leak at the brake booster or its hose is possible
result.now: Avoid driving it until the brakes are inspected. Have a mobile mechanic check it where it's parked, or have it towed to a shop.
if: If the pedal becomes very hard, sinks, or the red brake light comes on, don't move the car at all.
If the check engine light is on or the idle is rough, a leaking vacuum hose is more likely. Tell the shop.
result.why: The booster uses vacuum from the engine. A hiss when you press the pedal often means air is leaking in, either through a torn diaphragm inside the booster or a cracked hose or check valve. The leak reduces the assist and can also upset the engine's idle. A torn booster can get worse without warning.

causes.name: Torn booster diaphragm
causes.clues: The hiss comes from under the dash, near the pedal.

causes.name: Cracked vacuum hose or failed check valve
causes.clues: The hiss comes from under the hood, and the idle may be rough.

causes.name: Vacuum leak elsewhere on the engine
causes.clues: A rough idle or check engine light.
causes.against: If the hiss doesn't change when you press the brake, it's likely not the booster.

you: With a helper pressing the pedal, listen for where the hiss comes from.
Note whether the check engine light is on.

result.title: The power steering pump or drive belt may have stopped working, taking brake assist with it
result.now: Pull over when it's safe and stop driving. Have it towed.
if: If the battery light is on or the temperature gauge is climbing, a broken drive belt is likely. Turn the engine off and don't restart it.
If you see power steering fluid leaking or smell burning fluid, keep away from hot parts and tell the shop.
result.why: Some trucks, vans and diesel vehicles use a hydraulic brake booster powered by the power steering pump instead of engine vacuum. If the pump stops working, the steering and the brakes both get much heavier at once. On many engines, a broken belt also stops the alternator and water pump.

causes.name: Broken or slipping drive belt
causes.clues: A squeal beforehand, the battery light on, or the belt is missing.

causes.name: Low power steering fluid
causes.clues: A leak, or whining when you turn the wheel.

causes.name: Failed power steering pump or hydraulic booster
causes.clues: A whine, with the fluid level full.

you: With the engine off, look to see if the drive belt is still in place.
With the engine cold, check the power steering fluid level.

result.title: The brake booster may be losing some of its assist
result.now: Avoid driving it until the brakes are inspected. Have a mobile mechanic check it where it's parked, or have it towed to a shop.
if: If the pedal gets harder, sinks, or the red brake light comes on, don't move the car at all.
If it's hard mainly on the first press after the car has been parked, the check valve may be leaking vacuum. Mention that to the shop.
result.why: When the pedal is stiffer than usual but the car still stops with extra effort, the booster may be giving only part of its normal help. Common reasons are a weak booster, a leaking check valve or hose, or low engine vacuum. It can get worse over time, sometimes suddenly.

causes.name: Weak brake booster
causes.clues: The pedal barely drops when you start the engine.

causes.name: Leaking check valve or vacuum hose
causes.clues: The first press after parking is hard, then it improves.

causes.name: Low engine vacuum
causes.clues: A rough idle or other engine performance problems.

you: With the engine off, press the pedal several times, hold it down, then start the engine. It should sink slightly.

result.title: New pads may not be bedded in yet, or the brakes need a recheck
result.now: Before driving further, call the shop that did the work, describe what you notice, and ask them to recheck it. Many shops can come to you or arrange to bring the car in.
if: If it's much harder to stop than before the work, don't drive it. Ask the shop to check it right away.
If the shop tells you it's normal bedding-in for the pads they fitted, follow their bedding-in steps and have it rechecked if it isn't clearly better within a few drives.
If the pedal sinks or feels soft, or the red brake light comes on, don't drive it.
result.why: New pads and rotors need a number of moderate stops to lay down a thin layer of pad material on the rotor, called bedding in. Until then they can grip less. A shop will usually check pad seating, the calipers and the brake fluid before deciding anything needs to change.

causes.name: Pads not bedded in yet
causes.clues: Just replaced, and getting better day by day.

causes.name: Contaminated pads or rotors
causes.clues: Grease or fluid got on them during the job, often with squealing.

causes.name: Pad type or a caliper that isn't working properly
causes.clues: The car pulls to one side, or it's no better after several days.

you: Note whether braking improves over the next few drives.

result.title: The brakes may have overheated and lost grip (brake fade)
result.now: Pull over somewhere safe, set the parking brake and let the brakes cool for at least 30 minutes. Have the brakes checked before relying on them again.
if: If braking doesn't feel normal once the brakes are cool, or the pedal is soft, don't drive it. Have it towed.
Before moving the car again, call a shop or roadside assistance and describe what happened. If the brakes feel weak, soft or smell hot again at any point, stop and get help.
On long downhills, shift to a lower gear so the engine helps slow the car, instead of riding the brakes.
If you see smoke from a wheel, keep away from it until it cools.
result.why: Brake pads can only absorb so much heat. Constant or repeated braking, especially downhill or with a heavy load, overheats them so they grip less, and you often smell burning. They often recover once cool, but severe overheating can glaze the pads and damage the rotors, and very hot brakes can also boil the brake fluid.

causes.name: Overheated pads
causes.clues: A burning smell after long or hard braking.

causes.name: Glazed pads
causes.clues: Braking stays weak even after cooling, and the pads look shiny.

causes.name: Dragging brake adding heat
causes.clues: One wheel is much hotter than the others.

you: Once cool, test the brakes gently at low speed in an empty, safe area.

result.title: A stuck caliper or a problem on one side of the brakes is possible
result.now: Avoid driving it until the brakes are inspected. Have a mobile mechanic check it where it's parked, or have it towed to a shop.
if: If a wheel smokes or smells burning, keep away from it and let it cool.
If you see fluid at one wheel, or the pedal feels soft or sinks, don't move the car at all.
result.why: When one side does less of the braking, the car stops less effectively and pulls toward the side that's working. A stuck caliper, a collapsed brake hose, or contaminated pads on one side are common causes.

causes.name: Seized caliper or slide pins
causes.clues: One wheel is hotter, or its pads are worn unevenly.

causes.name: Collapsed brake hose
causes.clues: The pull comes and goes, or one wheel drags after braking.

causes.name: Contaminated pads on one side
causes.clues: Fluid or grease on that wheel.

you: Note which way the car pulls.
After a short drive, hold your hand near (not on) each wheel to compare heat.

result.title: Oil or brake fluid may have soaked the brakes on that wheel
result.now: Don't drive it. Have it towed so a shop can find the leak and check the brakes on that axle.
if: If it's brake fluid, the leak can also make the pedal soft or turn on the red brake light. Tell the shop what you've noticed.
If you see smoke or smell burning from that wheel, keep away from it and let it cool.
result.why: Brake pads lose much of their grip when oil, grease or brake fluid soaks into them, and it usually can't be reliably cleaned off, so a shop will often recommend new pads once the leak is confirmed. Fluid on a wheel also means something is leaking, and it may be the brake system itself.

causes.name: Leaking brake caliper or wheel cylinder
causes.clues: Wet fluid on the inside of the tire, and the brake fluid level is dropping.

causes.name: Leaking axle seal
causes.clues: Oily fluid at a rear wheel on a rear-wheel-drive vehicle, often with a gear-oil smell.

causes.name: Grease from a torn CV joint boot
causes.clues: Dark grease spattered inside a front wheel.
causes.against: This grease usually sprays around the wheel area rather than soaking the pads.

you: Look inside the wheel for wet spots without touching hot parts.
shop: Pad and rotor condition check on the affected axle

result.title: Your brakes may be worn or not working fully. Have them inspected before driving
result.now: Avoid driving it until the brakes are inspected. Have a mobile mechanic check it where it's parked, or have it towed to a shop.
if: If the pedal gets hard to press, sinks, or the red brake light comes on, don't move the car at all.
If you hear grinding when braking, the pads may be worn down to metal. Tell the shop.
If you smell burning or see smoke from a wheel, keep away from it and let it cool.
result.why: When the pedal feels normal but the car takes longer to stop, the problem is often at the wheels: worn or glazed pads, worn rotors, or a caliper that isn't working well. Worn tires can also lengthen stops. These get worse with time and can lead to bigger repairs.

causes.name: Worn pads or rotors
causes.clues: Squealing or grinding, or the brakes haven't been checked in a while.

causes.name: Glazed pads
causes.clues: Heavy braking or riding the brakes recently.

causes.name: Caliper not applying fully
causes.clues: Pulling to one side, or uneven pad wear.

causes.name: Worn tires
causes.clues: Little tread left, and stops feel worse on wet roads.

you: Look through the wheel spokes at the brake pad thickness if you can see it.
